stem: Regarding the accessory nerve, which of the following statements is INCORRECT:
options: The nerve originates from cervical segments C1–C5.
The nerve exits the skull through the jugular foramen.
The accessory nerve innervates the sternocleidomastoid and the trapezius muscle.
Accessory nerve palsy results in the inability to nod the head.
The nerve enters the cranial cavity through the foramen magnum.
fact: Accessory nerve palsy impairs shoulder shrugging and rotation of the head, not nodding. The spinal accessory nerve supplies sternocleidomastoid and trapezius and exits via the jugular foramen.
mnemonic: XI shrugs and turns: trapezius and SCM; nodding is not its main deficit.
finding: Source page displays inability to nod the head as the incorrect statement.

stem: The abducens nerve innervates which of the following muscles:
fact: The abducens nerve, CN VI, innervates the lateral rectus muscle and abducts the eye.
mnemonic: LR6: lateral rectus is supplied by CN VI.
finding: Source page displays lateral rectus as correct.

stem: A 35 year old woman presents to ED complaining of an inability to shrug her left shoulder or to turn her head to face the right side. The most likely injured nerve causing her symptoms exits the skull through which of the following:
fact: The spinal accessory nerve supplies trapezius and sternocleidomastoid and exits the skull through the jugular foramen.
mnemonic: Jugular foramen carries IX, X, XI; XI shrugs and turns the head.
finding: Source page displays jugular foramen as correct.

stem: A patient presents with an adducted eye at rest which cannot abduct past the midline, which of the following cranial nerves is most likely to be affected:
options: Ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve
fact: Abducens palsy causes an adducted, convergent eye because the lateral rectus cannot abduct the eye; severe palsy prevents abduction beyond the midline.
mnemonic: VI abducts; without it, medial rectus pulls the eye inward.
finding: Source page displays abducens nerve as correct.

stem: A 50 year old man presents to ED with diplopia and a ptosis. On pulling his eyelid up, you note that his pupil is looking down and out, and his pupil is fixed and dilated. Further imaging shows that the patient has a cerebral aneurysm compressing a cranial nerve. Which of the following blood vessels is most likely to be the culprit:
fact: A posterior communicating artery aneurysm can compress CN III, causing a fixed dilated pupil, ptosis, and a down-and-out eye.
mnemonic: PCom presses III: pupil, ptosis, and down-and-out eye.
finding: Source page displays posterior communicating artery as correct.

stem: Regarding the trochlear nerve, which of the following statements is CORRECT:
options: The trochlear nerve has both sensory and motor function.
The trochlear nerve innervates the superior rectus muscle.
The trochlear nerve has the shortest intracranial course.
The trochlear nerve enters the orbit through the superior orbital fissure.
Trochlear nerve palsy results in loss of eyeball adduction.
fact: The trochlear nerve is purely motor, supplies superior oblique, has the longest intracranial course, and enters the orbit through the superior orbital fissure.
mnemonic: CN IV enters through SOF and supplies SO: superior oblique.
finding: Source page displays entry through the superior orbital fissure as correct.

stem: A 55 year old woman presents to ED complaining of vertical diplopia with difficulty walking downstairs. She is tilting her head to one side as she says this helps ease the diplopia. Which of the following extraocular muscles is responsible for this picture:
fact: The superior oblique, supplied by CN IV, produces intorsion, depression, and abduction; its palsy causes vertical diplopia and difficulty walking downstairs.
mnemonic: SO4: superior oblique, CN IV, downgaze diplopia.
finding: Source page displays superior oblique as correct.

stem: The lingual nerve supplies which of the following:
options: Taste from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue
Sensation from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue
Sensation from the upper teeth and associated gingiva
fact: The lingual nerve carries general sensation from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue, oral floor, and lingual gingiva of the lower teeth. Chorda tympani carries taste fibres with it.
mnemonic: Lingual feels; chorda tympani tastes and stimulates saliva.
finding: Source page displays sensation from the anterior two-thirds of the tongue as correct.

stem: A patient presents with spontaneous onset of left sided facial weakness but is otherwise well. He is unable to purse his lips, close his eye fully or raise his eyebrow on the left side, which of the following is the most likely cause:
fact: An isolated lower-motor-neuron facial palsy involving the forehead, eyelid closure, and lower face is most commonly Bell's palsy when the patient is otherwise well.
mnemonic: Bell’s palsy affects the whole ipsilateral face, including the forehead.
finding: Source page displays Bell's palsy as correct.

stem: The glossopharyngeal nerve supplies general sensation to all of the following regions EXCEPT for:
fact: Upper teeth and associated gingiva are supplied by the maxillary division of the trigeminal nerve, not the glossopharyngeal nerve.
mnemonic: IX covers posterior tongue, tonsil, middle ear, and oropharynx; V2 covers upper teeth.
finding: Source page displays upper teeth and associated gingiva as the exception.
